title: Portrait and House
premise: Elodie Voss, a meticulous pest controller, is hired to clear Verrin House of an infestation that leaves human fingerprints in the dust. He documents everything—photos, sleep recordings, notes written like scripture—until the recordings reveal a second voice answering questions no one asked aloud. The house was not infested; it was invited, generations ago, by the Voss family itself, and Elodie's arrival has reactivated the contract. To survive until sunrise he must choose between destroying the house and the woman trapped inside it who loves him, or letting the inheritance complete itself through him.
about_author: Sable Eastwick is the pen name of a former building inspector from coastal Maine who spent a decade crawling through the attics and crawlspaces of old houses before turning to horror. Their fiction is known for procedural precision and the quiet dread of things found where they should not be.

chapters.title: Fingerprints in the Dust
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. Called to Verrin House for a 'rodent problem,' Elodie finds no droppings, no gnawing—only small human handprints pressed into attic dust, too fresh, too high on the walls. His instinct to document kicks in: photographs, measurements, timestamps. The beat is professional calm masking a first crack of unease; something in this house wants to be noticed.

chapters.title: The Client Who Won't Look Up
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. The client, Marguerite Verrin, hires him for thirty nights and forbids him from opening the sealed east bedroom. She never looks at the ceiling while speaking. Elodie sets up cameras and his old parabolic recorder near his cot in the kitchen. The beat is creeping obligation—he needs the money, and the house already feels like it expects him.

chapters.title: Documentation Is a Kind of Prayer
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. First week passes with nothing but cold spots and doors ajar by exactly four inches. Elodie's nightly ritual of logging findings becomes liturgical, almost comforting. Then he finds his own name written in the dust of the pantry floor—in handwriting that matches his late father's. The beat is the comfort of routine curdling into being watched.

chapters.title: The Second Voice
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. Reviewing his sleep recordings, Elodie hears himself talking at 3 a.m.—and a second voice, low and patient, answering questions he doesn't remember asking. It knows things about him it shouldn't. He plays the tape for Marguerite; she goes white and finally admits the east bedroom hasn't been opened since 1961. The beat is dread made audible.

chapters.title: What Was Invited In
chapters.summary: POV alternating Elodie/Marguerite. Marguerite confesses: her grandfather invited 'the tenant' into the house to save the family fortune, binding each heir to feed it secrets. Elodie realizes the Voss name on the deed traces back to his own family—the house called him home. The beat is the collapse of his identity as an outsider; he was always expected.

chapters.title: Thirty Nights, Twenty-Two Left
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. Elodie tries to leave; the road loops back to the house no matter which direction he drives. Inside, the handprints have multiplied and now include his own, made while he slept. He barricades the kitchen and keeps recording, because documentation is the only weapon he trusts. The beat is siege mentality—fear sharpened into method.

chapters.title: Marguerite's Bargain
chapters.summary: POV Marguerite. Marguerite reveals she was meant to be the tenant's next vessel and has been starving it for years by refusing to speak to it—but Elodie's voice is richer feeding than hers ever was. She offers him a way out: give it her instead, tonight. The beat is love against duty; she is offering sacrifice disguised as mercy, and he can't tell which she means.

chapters.title: The East Bedroom
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. With eight nights left, Elodie breaks the seal. Inside: decades of ledgers recording every secret fed to the house, ending with pages in his own handwriting dated after tonight. The tenant speaks to him directly now, offering his father's voice as payment for walking away. The beat is temptation—the corruption of power offered gently, like an inheritance.

chapters.title: Sunrise Clause
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. Final night. Elodie understands the contract's flaw: the house feeds on documented secrets, and his logs are its true body. He burns the ledgers and his own notebooks page by page while the house screams through every pipe and door, and Marguerite holds the line at the east bedroom, speaking to the tenant one last time to hold its attention. The beat is climax—love and duty fused into a single act of destruction.

chapters.title: Empty Rooms
chapters.summary: POV Elodie. Dawn. The house stands hollowed and silent, the handprints gone, Marguerite alive but unable to remember her grandfather's name—or much of anything the house took from her. Elodie drives away without looking back, though his recorder holds one final file: two voices laughing softly, neither of them his. The beat is bittersweet survival—freedom purchased, but the question of what still answers hanging open.
